variants.name: Async::Task on the fiber scheduler (community standard)
variants.idiom_name: Async (socketry) Async::Task + Async::Reactor over the Fiber Scheduler
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby's language-level primitive is the Fiber, and Ruby 3.0 added the Fiber Scheduler so an event loop can resume fibers that park on blocking calls; the dominant realization of a future is the Async gem, where Async::Task is a sequential computation you start and later wait on while Async::Reactor drives the fibers. The promise/future pair therefore lives in a library (task plus scheduler), not in the language, and the reactor stops child tasks when their scope ends; with stdlib alone the blocking approximation is Thread.new { ... }.value.
variants.code_sketch:
require "async"

Async do |task|                              # the reactor (scheduler)
  a = task.async { fetch_a(id) }             # Async::Task: the pending value
  b = task.async { fetch_b(id) }
  merged = merge(a.wait, b.wait)             # wait: the read end
end                                          # children stopped at block exit
pitfalls: A task whose exception nobody waits for is only reported late (to the reactor's error handler at best): every Async::Task needs a wait, a stop, or an explicit error sink - the fiber-scheduler equivalent of the dropped future.

Fiber-local storage changes where ambient state lives (Thread#[] is fiber-local while thread_variable_get is not), so libraries that stash per-request state behave differently under an async scheduler.

variants.name: Thread#value / Queue (stdlib blocking handle)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a fiber scheduler the stdlib idiom is one thread per pending value: Thread.new starts the producer and Thread#value joins it and returns the block's last expression, which is documented as the way to retrieve a thread's result, while a Queue gives the same one-shot handoff between threads. This is the classic structure written by hand and it is the right choice for I/O-bound work in ordinary request-per-thread Ruby; it is not a route to CPU parallelism, because the GVL still serialises Ruby execution.
variants.code_sketch:
pending = Thread.new { fetch(id) }     # producer (promise side)
other   = Thread.new { compute(id) }

value  = pending.value                  # joins and returns the result
value2 = other.value
# or hand off through a Queue if several consumers need the value
pitfalls: A thread whose value is never read keeps running unnoticed: the producer's failure surfaces nowhere near the requester (only through the thread's own report_on_exception path), so every thread needs a value/join or an explicit error sink.
Thread-per-pending-value stops scaling after a few dozen connections, and with the GVL it buys no CPU parallelism - bound the fan-out and move to a scheduler-based library for many concurrent waits.
